q: Describe two trends with distance inland.
Any two: organic matter and soil depth increase; pH falls; species number rises to 30, then falls.
Explain how early colonisers such as marram grass make the dunes suitable for later species.
Their roots bind the sand; when they die they add organic matter, which forms humus that holds water and nutrients; they also give shelter from wind and salt.
Suggest why the number of species falls at 1000 m.
Tall, dominant plants (pines or heath) shade out and outcompete others, and the soil becomes very acidic.
Explain why dunes are useful for studying succession.
Distance stands in for time, so all stages can be studied at once without waiting hundreds of years.
Suggest why the soil becomes more acidic inland.
Humus releases organic acids as it decomposes, and rain washes away the lime from shell fragments.
Compare the trends inside and outside the fence.
Inside, seedlings rise steadily from 2 to 65; outside they stay at 2–3.
Explain the difference.
Outside, deer browse the seedlings, killing most of them; inside, seedlings survive and grow.
Name the type of succession happening inside the fence, and explain why grazing stops it.
Secondary succession towards woodland. Grazing arrests it, keeping the land as grassland (a plagioclimax).
Predict what the inside plot will look like in 50 years. Explain.
Young woodland: trees grow tall and shade out many grassland plants.
Suggest why seedling numbers outside stay steady rather than falling to zero.
Seeds keep arriving and germinating each year; a few seedlings survive between visits by deer.
